content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to the adaptation process in the case-based reasoning paradigm by considering the failed cases. The experiment show that considering the failed cases in the adaptation process compared to the classical ones that ignore them can improve the performance of the casebased reasoning system.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

* The idea of utilizing failed cases is well motivated, interesting and intuitive. Results show that it can outperform classical methods with considering failed cases.

Weaknesses

* Experiments are only conducted on a single-data set, making results less convincing.
* As case-based reasoning systems, more experiments under different tasks should be evaluated and discussed. The main paper, however, only presents results within a single table.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Conventional adaptation processes in a case-based reasoning (CBR) system consider only successful
source cases to improve its performance. The paper claims to introduce a more novel perspective, where both
successful and failed cases are considered. Drawing on the intuition that failed cases also hold
useful knowledge, the experiments performed demonstrate that considering failed cases also improve
the overall performance of CBR systems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
● Generalization is an important consideration for AI and CBR is a well studied approach towards it. A notable strength
 of this paper is that it contributes to a very promising, albeit niche, area of research.
The authors claim only one other work that considers positive and negative cases. 
● The authors make use of the LOOCV approach over the validation set and lower the bias
generated within the models, since they are repeatedly fitted on different datasets.
● The experiment setup and evaluation are clear to follow, though it is unclear how the usage
of four different baselines have any other effects on model learning.

Weaknesses:
* In contrast to the author's claims on positive cases only for CBR, there is a long history of work on negative examples. This was for explanation based learning (EBL) and in particular, when failure was used to generate explanations. See for example, work on planning and cases - https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/jair/pub/volume7/ihrig97a-html/. EBL should be discussed in general, and put in the context of this work.
● The paper claims that this approach may be used in any domain-independent context. However,
this might require using very general adaptation rules, which may produce overfitted (or
incorrect) results. How is this addressed? It is also unclear as to how the approach allows
for domain-independent CBR studies. While very specific adaptation rules may be cumbersome
and useless in complex systems, extremely general rules may suffer from inaccuracy.
● It is unclear as to how the real and semi-synthetic datasets were generated and collected.
● A drawback of this paper is that there is not a guarantee that a successful solution can
always be found, especially if the source cases may be failed ones. The authors also address
this.
* The proportion of negative and positive cases needed for effective solving should be discussed.
● The authors only consider one domain of work (energy management in a building), but do not
discuss any others, where further fine-tuning of failed/negative cases may be necessary.
● Spelling/grammar errors and word/equation formatting errors. Another round of proofreading is
necessary.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is mostly well written. But the structure is somewhat confusing to follow (e.g., some crucial related work mentioned within appendix, unclear information about generation of datasets). There are also many typos (e.g., “equation
equation 3”) and grammatical tense errors.
*
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper looks at CBR and claims to improve it by considering both positive and negative cases. However, they do not consider old work in CBR/EBL that use negative cases for explanations. They discuss  a single case study which needs to be extended. The writing needs to be improved.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an approach to the adaptation process learning from both failed and successful cases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:

This paper is not well written, which makes it difficult to understand. For example, this paper states “Existing adaptation approaches focus exclusively on cases whose solutions are deemed relevant to the corresponding problems … ” but they did not give any citation about “existing adaptation approaches” in this sentence. In addition, the sentence “despite a large number of research studies and an increased interest in the adaptation issue” does not have citations to support this “large number of research studies”. There are more sentences without citations in this article, which makes this paper does not meet the standard of academic writing. 

This paper doesn’t introduce [1] thoroughly in its Preliminaries section despite [1] being the most relevant paper announced by this paper. I originally planned to read [1], but it needs to be paid and this article does not introduce it in detail, which makes it troublesome to understand. 


*References*

[1]. Jean Lieber and Emmanuel Nauer. Adaptation knowledge discovery using positive and negative cases. In Antonio A. Sanchez-Ruiz and Michael W. Floyd (eds.), ´ Case-Based Reasoning Research and Development, pp. 140–155, Cham, 2021. Springer International Publishing. ISBN 978-3-030- 86957-1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Reproducibility:

I did not see any open source code, which makes it hard to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents an improved adaptation process by reasoning from failed and successful cases. Language models also have some relevant papers about learning from failed cases, which is an interesting topic. But due to writing problems, this paper is hard to understand.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach for case based reasoning that utilizes both similar successful and similar unsuccessful cases. The idea is motivated from the perspective of robotic navigation, where the target generates an attractive force and obstacles generate repulsive forces. Similarly, here, successful cases become attractive forces whereas unsuccessful cases become repulsive forces. Promising results are shown on an energy management system problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---

- The proposed method is relatively simple and performs well on the energy management system experiment.

Weaknesses
---

- It is difficult to judge the empirical contribution as there is only one experiment shown.
- The paper is somewhat difficult to follow, delegating too much space to motivation and not enough to technical details (see below).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality
---

The main concern I have with the quality of the work is that there is only one experiment. To fully verify the soundness and strengths of the proposed approach, more experiments should be carried out, ideally in diverse real-world settings. Are the settings considered in CBR-R paper feasible here?

Clarity
---

The paper is difficult to follow. Mainly, I do not believe that it is best to motivate the approach from the artificial potential field perspective. Indeed, Section 3.3 has a long list of ways in which the proposed method differs. I would recommend removing the digression into robotic path planning and instead using the space to present the proposed method in greater detail.

Originality
---

I am not an expert in this area, so it is difficult for me to judge the novelty and originality of this work.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, there are several important improvements that can be made as laid out above. I am recommending weak reject and am happy to discuss further.

content.title: Improve the Adaptation Process by Reasoning From Failed and Successful Cases
content.TL;DR: This work presents a new approach to the adaptation process in the case-based reasoning paradigm
content.abstract:
Usually, existing works on adaptation in reasoning-based systems assume that the case base holds only successful cases, i.e., cases having solutions believed to be appropriate for the corresponding problems. However, in practice, the case base could hold failed cases, resulting from an earlier adaptation process but discarded by the revision process. Not considering failed cases would be missing an interesting opportunity to learn more knowledge for improving the adaptation process.
This paper proposes a novel approach to the adaptation process in the case-based reasoning paradigm, based on an improved barycentric approach by considering the failed cases.The experiment performed on real data demonstrates the benefit of the method considering the failed cases in the adaptation process compared to the classical ones that ignore them, thus, improving  the performance of the case-based reasoning system.
